The pale rice-paper lantern has a torn vertical seam neatly joined with visible blue cotton stitches over its bamboo ribs; crumpled wet paper and a loose hoop on the bench explain what she has just rescued. Her right hand holds a smartphone upright beside and below her face, its rear camera aimed into a tall physical mirror and its screen facing her. Her left hand grips the lantern's rigid bamboo carrying handle at waist height, with the fingers visibly wrapping the handle and the lantern hanging clear of her body. Her elbows remain relaxed and bent; her planted stance leaves both hands free for their separate tasks. She checks the phone screen with a tired, small smile, the unclenched mouth and softened brow making the completed repair feel quietly worth recording. A simple rust-colored cotton work shirt and a fine loose strand against her cheek support her particular presence. The photograph is captured by the phone's rear camera through the mirror: its weathered wooden frame bounds the reflection, and the reflected workbench stays spatially continuous behind her. A medium three-quarter crop retains her face, both working hands, the entire lantern and the damaged paper. Cool rainy window light and one warm bench lamp reveal paper fibers, stitch tension, realistic skin texture and the recovered lantern's dry translucent surface. The lantern and her face carry the attention; the subdued workshop traces supply the reason for her relief.
